en: The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra: Now, therefore, we shall explain dharma. That from which the attainment of prosperity (abhyudaya) and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) results is dharma.
From his word follows the authority of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind are the substances.
Color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognitions, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are the qualities (*guṇa*).
Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion are the actions (*karman*).

(KVs 1.1.6) "Existent," "non-eternal," "possessing substance," "effect," "cause," and "possessing generality and particularity"—these are the common characteristics of substances, qualities, and actions. (KVs 1.1.7)
Substances originate another substance; qualities originate another quality;
action is not found to be accomplished by action.
Substance is non-contradictory to both effect and cause;
(KVs 1.1.11) quality is likewise [non-contradictory] to both;
(KVs 1.1.12) action is contradictory to effect. (KVs 1.1.13)
"Having action, having quality, and being an inherent cause" is the definition of substance (dravya). KVs 1.1.14.
"Residing in a substance, devoid of qualities, and not being a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions while being independent" is the definition of quality (guṇa). KVs 1.1.15.
"Residing in a single substance, devoid of qualities, and being an independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions" is the definition of action (karman). KVs 1.1.16.
Substance is the common cause of substances, qualities, and actions (KVs 1.1.17).
Likewise, quality [is the common cause] (KVs 1.1.18).
Action is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions (KVs 1.1.19).
Not because of the distinction between substances;
not because of the difference in properties from qualities, nor from actions;
for substances, the effect is a substance, which is the universal.

Numbers beginning with duality, as well as separateness, conjunction, and disjunction [do not have substance as their effect], because they do not reside in it by way of inherence (asamavāya). Universals and action do not exist as effects [of substance].
Conjunctions have substance as their effect.
The commonality of material forms is "material form" (rūpa). The commonality of heaviness, effort, and conjunction is "throwing upward" (utkṣepaṇa).
The commonality of actions is "conjunctions and disjunctions" (saṃyoga-vibhāga).

In the general case of causes, it has been stated that among substances and actions, action is not a cause [of another action]. (KVs 1.1.29) From the absence of a cause follows the absence of the effect;
(KVs 1.2.1) but from the absence of the effect, there is no absence of the cause. (KVs 1.2.2)
"Universal" and "particular" are relative to cognition.
(KVs 1.2.3) Being (*bhāva*) is only a universal. (KVs 1.2.4) Substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*) are both universals and particulars. (KVs 1.2.5)
Except for the ultimate particularities (antyaviśeṣas).
[KVs 1.2.6] That from which the notion "existent" arises with respect to substances, qualities, and actions;
[KVs 1.2.7] existence (sattā) is an entity distinct from substances, qualities, and actions. [KVs 1.2.8]
It is not a substance because it possesses a single substance [as its substratum] (KVs 1.2.9);
nor is it an action or a quality because it exists in qualities and actions (KVs 1.2.10);
and also because of the absence of universals and particulars (KVs 1.2.11).
Substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is stated [to be excluded] because of having a single substance as its locus (KVs 1.2.12),
and because of the absence of generalities and particularities (KVs 1.2.13). Quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is stated [to be excluded] because of its presence in a quality (KVs 1.2.14).
And because of the absence of both generality and particularity.
(KVs 1.2.15) Since it exists in the object, "object-ness" is stated.
(KVs 1.2.16) And because of the absence of both generality and particularity. (KVs 1.2.17)
Because there is no distinction in their general characteristics and because there is an absence of specific characteristics, substance is one.
Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch.
Water possesses color, taste, and touch; it is fluid and viscous.
Fire possesses color and tangibility.
Wind possesses tangibility.
These do not exist in space.

The commonality among earthy substances such as clarified butter, lac, and beeswax, in their state of liquefaction due to contact with fire, is with water. (KVs 2.1.6) The commonality among metallic substances such as tin, lead, iron, silver, and gold, in their state of liquefaction due to contact with fire, is with water.
(KVs 2.1.7) "Having horns," "having a hump," "having a tail-tip at the end," and "having a dewlap"—these are observed as the marks for the universal *gotva* (cowness). (KVs 2.1.8)
And there is touch.
Since there is no touch of those things that are seen, air has an unperceived mark.
Because it lacks the quality of being a substance, it is a substance. (C, V)
[The eternality of space is established] by its being devoid of substance (adravyavattvena) / [as stated in] KVs 2.1.11;

and because it possesses action and possesses qualities (kriyāvattvād guṇavattvāc ca) / [as stated in] KVs 2.1.12; its eternality has been declared by virtue of its being devoid of substance (adravyavattvena nityatvam uktam) / [as stated in] C and BhV.
(V impermanent because it is not a substance,
U because it is not a substance) / KVs_2,1.13 / The mingling of winds with wind is a mark of plurality. KVs_2,1.14 /
Regarding the statement "of air" (vāyoḥ): since there is no perception [of air] despite its proximity, no directly perceived mark (liṅga) exists.
From the "generally observed" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa) type of inference as well, there is no distinction [to establish it]. Therefore, [the existence of air] is known through scripture (āgamika).
The act of naming, however, is a mark of those superior to us;
for the act of naming is preceded by direct perception.
Going out and entering are the marks of space.
Therefore, that [sound] is not a mark [of conjunction], because action resides in a single substance;
and because it differs from the non-perception of other causes;
and because of the destruction of action through conjunction.

A quality in an effect is seen to be preceded by a quality in its cause; and because no other effect [of sound] arises, sound is not a quality of tangible substances. Because it inheres in something else and because it is perceptible, it is neither a quality of the self nor a quality of the mind.
It is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of space.

Substantiality and permanence are explained by [the case of] air. Reality [is established] through existence. When there is contact between a flower and a cloth, the non-appearance of another odor in the cloth is the mark of the absence of odor in the cloth.
By this, the heat in water is explained.
(KVs 2.2.2) Odor is established in earth; heat in fire. (KVs 2.2.3–4)
Coldness is the quality of water (KVs 2.2.5).
"The other [is] prior," "simultaneous," "not simultaneous," "long duration," and "quick"—these are the marks of time (KVs 2.2.6).
Its substantiality and eternity are explained by [the discussion on] air (KVs 2.2.7).
Reality is by way of its essence;
diversity is by way of specific effects.
[This is so] because [diversity] is absent in eternal things and present in non-eternal things.

The designation "time" (kāla) is used for the cause [of priority and posteriority]. That from which [one perceives] "this is from that" is the indicative mark (liṅga) of direction (diś). Its substantiality (dravyatva) and eternity (nityatva) are explained by [the discussion of] air (vāyu).
The reality [of direction] is by way of its essential nature (bhāva);
diversity [of direction] is by way of specific effects.
The "eastern" direction is so called because of its connection with the sun, whether that connection has previously occurred, will occur in the future, or is currently occurring.
Likewise [the notions of] south, west, and north [arise].
By this, the intermediate directions are explained.
Doubt arises from the perception of a common property, the non-perception of specific properties, and the recollection of specific properties.
The seen is the unseen (KVs 2.2.20).
And the seen is like the seen (KVs 2.2.21).
The seen is the seen as it was, the seen as it was not, and the seen in both ways, because of its being seen in both ways (KVs 2.2.22).
And from [the consideration of] knowledge and ignorance, there arises doubt.
(KVs 2.2.23) That object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing is sound.
(KVs 2.2.24) Regarding that [sound], there is doubt as to whether it is a substance, an action, or a quality. (KVs 2.2.25)
Because a particularity (viśeṣa) is observed in both ways—among things of the same class and among things that are different in nature.
(KVs 2.2.26) It is not a substance because it inheres in a single substance. (KVs 2.2.27) It is not action because it is not visible to the eye. (KVs 2.2.28)
The release of an existing quality through actions shares a commonality with [the state of] karma;
because there is no mark (liṅga) of its existence;
and because it possesses the characteristic of being unlike that which is eternal.
Because it is an effect;
because of non-existence;
because of the modification of the cause.
Because of a defect;
because sound is produced from conjunction, from disjunction, and from another sound;
and because of an inferential mark, it is non-eternal.
Because there is an absence of two occurrences [of the operation],
because of the absence of number,
and because of the word "first" (prathama). (KVs 2.2.38–40)
And because there is an absence of agreement [regarding them],
[the objects] are doubtful when there is a plurality of existents (KVs 2.2.41).
There is an absence of number in a general sense (KVs 2.2.42–43).

The sense objects are well-known. (KVs 3.1.1) The fact that the sense objects are well-known is the reason for their being distinct from the senses. (KVs 3.1.2) That [reason] is not a valid indicator. (KVs 3.1.3)
Due to ignorance of the cause (KVs 3.1.4),
due to ignorance of the effect (KVs 3.1.5),
and due to ignorance [itself] (KVs 3.1.6).
"That which is a different cause is not a valid reason" (KVs 3.1.7).

[The types of reasons are: the conjoined (*saṃyogin*), the inherent (*samavāyin*), the inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*), the contradictory (*virodhin*), and the effect (*kārya*) of another effect.
A cause [is the opposite] of another cause;
the non-existent is the opposite of the existent, and the existent is the opposite of the non-existent.
The non-existent [is the reason] for the non-existent,
and the existent for the existent;
for a logical indicator (apadeśa) is preceded by what is well-established.

That which is unestablished is not a valid reason (*anapadeśa*). (KVs 3.1.10) That which is non-existent and that which is doubtful are also not valid reasons. (KVs 3.1.11) For example: "It is a horse because it has horns," and "It is a cow because it has horns. (KVs 3.1.12)
That which is produced from the contact of the self, the sense organs, the mind, and the object is [cognition] distinct [from the self].
(KVs 3.1.13) Activity and cessation [of activity] are observed in the internal self; these are the marks [indicating the existence] of another [the external self].
(KVs 3.1.14) The non-existence and existence of cognition when there is contact between the self, the sense organs, and the object are the marks of the mind. (KVs 3.2.1)
Substantiality and eternity are explained by [the discussion of] air (KVs 3.2.2).
Because of the non-simultaneity of effort and the non-simultaneity of cognitions, the mind is one (KVs 3.2.3).

Inhalation and exhalation, opening and closing of the eyes, life, movements of the mind, modifications of the other sense organs, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, and effort—these are the marks of the self (KVs 3.2.4).
Substantiality and permanence are explained by [the case of] air (KVs 3.2.5).
In the case of [a person named] Yajñadatta, since there is no perception despite the presence of sensory contact, no perceived mark (*liṅga*) exists (KVs 3.2.6).
And from the "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), there is no distinction [to establish his specific identity] (KVs 3.2.7).
Therefore, [the self] is based on scripture (āgamika).
Because it is distinct from the word "I," it is not based on scripture.
Furthermore, if [the self were perceptible], one would directly perceive it as "I am Devadatta" or "I am Yajñadatta."

In expressions such as "Devadatta goes" or "Viṣṇumitra goes," [the self] is perceived through the body by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra). However, this metaphorical designation is doubtful.
Because the notion of "I" exists with respect to the internal self (pratyagātman) but does not exist with respect to anything else, it is the perception of a distinct entity (arthāntara).

But there is no difference in knowledge between Yajñadatta and Viṣṇumitra due to a difference in their bodies. (KVs 3.2.14) There is a single self because there is no difference in the production of pleasure, pain, and cognition.
(KVs 3.2.15) [The self is] manifold because of the established order [of experiences]. (KVs 3.2.16)
And from the authority of the treatises:
"That which exists without a cause is eternal" (KVs 3.2.17); "Its effect is its mark" (KVs 4.1.1). "The effect is its mark" (KVs 4.1.2).
For the existence of the effect follows from the existence of the cause (KVs 4.1.3).
And "impermanent" is the state of negating a specific [permanence] (KVs 4.1.4).
And ignorance [is the cause] (KVs 4.1.5).

In the case of a large [substance], there is perception because it possesses multiple constituent substances and because of its color-form (rūpa). (KVs 4.1.6) In the case of an atom, there is no perception because it does not possess [multiple] constituent substances.
(KVs 4.1.7) In the case of air, there is no perception because of the absence of the formation of color-form (rūpa-saṃskāra). (KVs 4.1.8)
Perception [of color] occurs due to its inherence in a substance composed of multiple substances and due to a specific quality of color.
By this, the cognition of taste, smell, and touch is explained.
Because of the absence of those [other qualities], there is no deviation [in the rule].
Number, dimensions, separateness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, and action—these are visible because they are inherent in substances possessing color.
(KVs 4.1.12) They are not visible in those [substances] lacking color.
(KVs 4.1.13) By this, the perception of all [qualities] through their respective sense organs is explained in the case of both quality-ness and existence. (KVs 4.1.14)

Because conjunction is imperceptible with respect to both perceptible and imperceptible things, that which consists of five elements does not exist; and because no other quality arises, that which consists of three elements also does not exist. However, the mutual conjunction of the five [elements] with the self is not prohibited.
Because it is preceded by many locations;
because of the distinction of the property (*dharma*);
because of the distinction of the effect (*kārya*).
Because there is an absence of traditional designation (KVs_4,2.7);
because they possess names and so forth (KVs_4,2.8);
and because there are those born not from a womb, as evidenced by the marks in the Vedas (KVs_4,2.9).
Action in the hand arises from both self-conjunction and effort (KVs_5,1.1).
Likewise, action in the pestle arises from conjunction with the hand (KVs_5,1.2).
However, in the case of action in the pestle produced by impact, conjunction with the hand is not the cause because of its absence [in that specific instance] (KVs_5,1.3).

Likewise, in the case of the action of the hand and the pestle, there is conjunction with the self [of the hand] during the action of the hand and pestle. (KVs 5.1.4) But from the blow of the pestle—that is, from the conjunction with the pestle—action arises in the hand. (KVs 5.1.5) Similarly, [action arises] in the self from its conjunction with the hand. (KVs 5.1.6)
In the absence of conjunction, falling occurs due to gravity (KVs 5.1.7).
Due to the absence of a specific impulse, there is no upward or horizontal motion (KVs 5.1.8).
A specific impulse arises from a specific effort (KVs 5.1.9).
From a particular kind of pushing arises a particular kind of throwing upward.
By the action of the hand, the action of the child is explained.
Likewise is the bursting of that which is burnt.
In the absence of effort, the falling of a sleeping person occurs due to gravity (KVs_5,1.13).
The movement of grass is due to contact with the wind (KVs_5,1.14).
The movement of a jewel and the gliding of a needle are caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) (KVs_5,1.15).

In the case of an arrow, specific conjunctions occurring non-simultaneously are the cause for the diversity of its actions. (KVs 5.1.16) The first action of the arrow arises from an impulsion; subsequent actions arise from the momentum produced by that action, and each following action likewise arises from momentum. (KVs 5.1.17) In the absence of momentum, falling occurs due to gravity. (KVs 5.1.18)
Action in earth arises from pushing, striking, and conjunction with that which is conjoined;
it is produced specifically by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
In the case of water, falling occurs due to gravity when there is an absence of conjunction [with something else].
That [motion] is specifically caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
Flowing occurs due to fluidity (dravatva).
Ascent occurs due to the conjunction of air with the stalk.

From impulsion, from pressure, and from conjunction with that which is conjoined [with the cause], there is the upward movement of trees; this is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). The solidification of water and the melting of fire result from conjunction.
In that context, thunder is the indicative mark (liṅga) [of the deity];
and it is Vedic.
Thunder arises from the conjunction and disjunction of waters.
By means of the action of earth, the action of fire and the action of air are explained.
(KVs 5.2.13) The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of air, and the initial motion of atoms and the mind are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
(KVs 5.2.14) By means of the action of the hand, the action of the mind is explained. (KVs 5.2.15)

Pleasure and pain arise from the contact of the self, the sense organs, the mind, and their objects; the non-occurrence of these is [the goal]. (KVs 5.2.16) When the mind is situated in the self, there is an absence of pleasure and pain for one who possesses a body; that is *yoga*. (KVs 5.2.17) By means of bodily action, the action of the self is explained. (KVs 5.2.18)
Withdrawal, movement toward, the conjunction of what has been eaten and drunk, and conjunctions with other effects—these are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
In the absence of that [unseen force], there is an absence of conjunction, which is non-manifestation; that is liberation (*mokṣa*).
Darkness is merely the absence of existence, because it possesses characteristics different from substance, quality, and action.
And because light is obstructed by other substances.
Space, time, and ether are devoid of action because they possess properties contrary to those that possess action.
By this, actions and qualities are also explained [as being devoid of action].
The inherence of inactive [substances] is prohibited by [the rules on] actions (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 5.2.25).
But qualities that do not inhere [in a substance] are the cause [of its cognition] (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 5.2.26).
Space is explained by means of [the same] qualities (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 5.2.27).
Time is established by its cause.
(KVs 5.2.28) The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence.
(KVs 6.1.1) And there is no mark [of authorship] for the seer other than our own intelligences. (KVs 6.1.2)

Likewise, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, the accomplishment of the act of naming is a mark [of his status]. (KVs 6.1.3) Giving preceded by conscious intent [is a mark of his status]. (KVs 6.1.4) Likewise, receiving [is a mark of his status]. (KVs 6.1.5)

The sequence of these two is as follows: [it applies] to those things that are not mutually constituent parts (aṅga) of one another, because the qualities of one self are not the cause of the qualities of another self. Prosperity arises from eating wholesome food and from associating with such people.
That [fault] does not exist in the case of eating what is spoiled (duṣṭabhojana).
For "spoiled" (duṣṭa) refers to injury (hiṃsā).
The fault arises from the association [of the words].
That [desire] does not exist in one who is not defiled (aduṣṭa).
Its engagement is toward what is distinguished;
it does not engage with what is equal or inferior.
By this, taking from righteous persons who are inferior, equal, or superior has been explained (KVs 6.1.15).
Likewise, the abandonment of those who are hostile (KVs 6.1.16). In the case of equals, it is either self-sacrifice or the sacrifice of others (KVs 6.1.17).
In special cases, there is the renunciation of life.
(KVs 6.1.18) The performance of those things whose purposes are seen, when their visible purpose is absent, leads to prosperity.
(KVs 6.2.1) [Variant: The performance of those things whose purposes are both seen and unseen, when the seen purpose is absent, leads to prosperity.]

Consecration, fasting, celibacy, residence in the teacher’s house, the life of a forest hermit, sacrifice, giving, sprinkling, and the observances regarding direction, lunar mansion, mantra, and time are for the sake of the unseen (transcendental merit).
The four stages of life (āśrama) arise from both the presence and the absence of *upadhā*.
*Upadhā* is a defect of intention.
The absence of defects is non-defilement (anupadhā).
That which possesses desirable form, taste, smell, and touch, and has been consecrated by sprinkling or poured over with water, is pure.
"Impure" is the negation of "pure."

And there is a difference in meaning. (KVs 6.2.8) For one who is not self-restrained, spiritual elevation does not arise from eating pure food, because of the absence of restraint. (KVs 6.2.9) Yet it does arise, because restraint is not something other [than purity]. (KVs 6.2.10)
And because it does not exist when [the object] is absent;
attachment arises from pleasure;
because one becomes absorbed in that [pleasure].
From satisfaction;
from the unseen (adṛṣṭa);
and from the particularity of genus, there arises a particularity of passion.
Activity toward merit and demerit is preceded by desire and aversion (KVs_6.2.17).
From that arise conjunction and disjunction (KVs_6.2.18).
Liberation regarding the actions of the self has been explained (KVs_6.2.19).
The qualities have been stated;
the definition of a quality has been stated;
and it has been stated that "this possesses such qualities" and "that possesses such qualities."
On earth, color, taste, odor, and tangibility are impermanent because their substance is impermanent;
(KVs_7,1.4) and also because of contact with fire;
(KVs_7,1.5) and because of the manifestation of other qualities. (KVs_7,1.6)
By this, non-eternality in eternal [substances] has been stated.
(KVs 7.1.7) In water, fire, and air, [number] is eternal because the substance is eternal. (KVs 7.1.8) In non-eternal [substances], it is non-eternal because the substance is non-eternal. (KVs 7.1.9)

On earth, qualities are preceded by the qualities of their causes, as are those produced by heating (pākaja). In water, fire, and air, qualities are preceded by the qualities of their causes, but those produced by heating do not exist.
Because qualities are initiated in a substance that is itself devoid of [prior] qualities, action and quality are themselves without qualities.
By this, qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*) are explained [as being non-eternal],
because they reside in a single substance (KVs 7.1.13).
The perception and non-perception of the minute (*aṇu*) and the large (*mahat*) are explained as being [the criteria for] the eternal (KVs 7.1.14–15).
Large [dimension] arises from a multiplicity of causes, from the largeness of the cause, and from a specific accumulation.
Its opposite is minute.
[The distinction between] "minute" and "large" exists because of the presence of specific qualities in that [object] and the absence of such specific qualities [in the other].
Because they exist at the same time.
(KVs 7.1.19) The absence of minuteness and magnitude in [the qualities of] minuteness and magnitude is explained by [the analysis of] actions and qualities.
(KVs 7.1.21) Actions and qualities are devoid of [the qualities of] minuteness and magnitude because of [their own lack of] minuteness and magnitude. (KVs 7.1.22)
By this, longness and shortness are explained.
(Kāśikāvṛtti 7.1.23) Actions [are compared] with actions, and qualities with qualities.
(Kāśikāvṛtti 7.1.24) That [comparison] applies when [the objects] are non-eternal. (Kāśikāvṛtti 7.1.25)
Eternal and spherical. Ignorance is the mark of knowledge. Space is great because of its pervasiveness.
And so too is the self (ātman).
Because of its absence [in the case of atoms], the mind (manas) is atomic. Space (diś) is explained by means of its qualities (guṇa).
Time is [defined] by its causal function.
(KVs 7.1.32) Unity is a distinct entity from color, taste, smell, and touch; likewise is separateness.
(KVs 7.2.1) Their permanence and impermanence are explained by the [same criteria applied to] the color and touch of fire. (KVs 7.2.2)
And [the definition of] accomplishment is as follows:
there is an absence of unity and plurality in both unity and plurality;
actions [are established] by means of actions, and qualities by means of qualities.
Because the qualities of karma are innumerable, there is no such thing as universal oneness (sarvaikatva).
Because oneness does not exist, figurative designation (bhākta) does not exist. Due to the absence of unity or plurality between cause and effect, neither unity nor plurality exists.

This has explained the impermanent and the permanent. (KVs 7.2.9) Conjunction is born from the action of one [of two things], born from the action of both, and born from conjunction. (KVs 7.2.10) By this, disjunction is explained. (KVs 7.2.11)
The absence of conjunction and disjunction in conjunction and disjunction themselves is explained by the [absence of] minuteness and magnitude.
Actions [are devoid of them] through actions, and qualities through qualities.
Because there is no separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*) between cause and effect, conjunction and disjunction do not exist [between them].
Because it is a quality (guṇatvāt);
because it is spoken of as a quality (guṇe ca bhāṣyate);
because it is devoid of action (niṣkriyatvāt).
Because of the usage [of the words] "existent" and "non-existent," the word and its object are unconnected (asaṃbaddha),
[as in the case of] a staff [known] from one who possesses it through conjunction (saṃyoga), or a horn [known] from one who possesses it through inherence (samavāya). (KVs 7.2.18–20)
Because it is observed [to exist], the condition (*pratyaya*) is not the cause (*ahetu*). Likewise, there is an absence of conditions (*pratyayābhāva*).
If it is argued that [the effect exists] because of a connection with what is connected (*saṃbaddhasaṃbandhāt*), then there is doubt (*sandeha*).
The cognition of meaning from a word is conventional (sāmayika).
[The notions of] "far" and "near" arise with respect to two things situated in the same direction and time, which are respectively distant and proximate;
this is due to the priority of the cause and the posteriority of the cause.

The absence of remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) in [the qualities of] remoteness and proximity is explained by [the absence of] minuteness (*aṇutva*) and magnitude (*mahattva*). Actions [are absent] in actions, and qualities [are absent] in qualities.
That from which [there arises the cognition] "here" with respect to cause and effect is inherence (*samavāya*).
The negation of substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness has been explained by means of existence (bhāva).
[KVs 7.2.30] And so too their actual nature (tattva).
[KVs 7.2.31] Cognition regarding substances has been explained. [KVs 8.1]
The mind and the self [are also causes].
(KVs 8.2) In the exposition of knowledge, the production of knowledge has been stated.
(KVs 8.3) Regarding qualities and actions that are not in contact [with the senses], because knowledge is produced, the substance is the cause and the cause of the cause. (KVs 8.4)

In the case of generalities and particulars, cognition arises from those very [generalities and particulars] because of the absence of further generalities and particulars within them. (KVs 8.5) Cognition regarding substances, qualities, and actions depends upon generalities and particulars.
(KVs 8.6) Regarding a substance, cognition depends upon substances, qualities, and actions. (KVs 8.7)
Because qualities and actions lack [intrinsic] qualities and actions, there is no dependence upon qualities and actions [for their own cognition].

(KVs 8.8) From the whiteness inherent in a substance arises the cognition of whiteness; from that [cognition of whiteness] arises the cognition of the white [substance]; these two stand in a cause-and-effect relationship.
(KVs 8.9) This is because substances do not act as causes for one another, and because their causes do not arise simultaneously. (KVs 8.10)

Likewise, [the notion of "this"] applies to substances, qualities, and actions because there is no difference in their causes. (KVs 8.11) This [notion], such as "This was done by you; feed him," is dependent upon cognition.
(KVs 8.12) Because it exists when [objects] are perceived and does not exist when they are not perceived. (KVs 8.13)
"Object" (*artha*) refers to substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*).
Regarding substances, that which consists of five elements has been explained [previously].
Earth is the cause for the cognition of odor because of its abundance and its possession of odor.
Likewise, water, fire, and air [are established] through the specific qualities of taste, form, and touch in the cognitions of taste, form, and touch.
[The unmanifest is] non-existent because of the absence of activity, quality, and designation;
it is both existent and non-existent.
Because non-existence lacks action, qualities, and designation, it is a different entity from existence.
(KVs 9.3) That which exists is both existent and non-existent. (KVs 9.4) And that which is other than existence is also non-existent. (KVs 9.5)
The cognition "it is non-existent" arises because there is no perception of the real thing, because there is memory of the real thing, and because there is perception of its opposite;
likewise, it arises because there is perception of existence when that [thing] is absent.
By this, the cases of "non-pot," "non-cow," and "non-dharma" are explained.
"Non-existent" (abhūtam) and "does not exist" (nāsti) are not different in meaning. "There is no jar in the house" is a negation of the conjunction of an existing jar with the house.
"There is no other moon" is a negation of [an object] other than the moon in its general sense.
Because of the difference in nature between the existent and the non-existent, there is no existence or non-existence in the effect [of the same kind].
(KVs 9.12) The perception of the self arises from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind within the self. (KVs 9.13) Likewise, it occurs with respect to other substances. (KVs 9.14)
And [perception arises] from the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object (KVs 9.15);
from inherence in that [object], [it arises] with respect to actions and qualities (KVs 9.16);
and from inherence in the self, [it arises] with respect to the qualities of the self (KVs 9.17).

"This is the effect of that," "this is the cause of that," "this is related to that," "this inheres in the same object as that," and "this is contradictory to that"—such is inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika*).
By this, verbal knowledge (*śābda*) is explained.
Cause (*hetu*), indicator (*apadeśa*), mark (*liṅga*), motive (*nimitta*), means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and reason (*kāraṇa*) are synonymous.
Because it depends on the cognition "this belongs to that" (KVs 9.21);
memory arises from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, and from mental impressions (saṃskāra) (KVs 9.22);
likewise for dreaming and the state immediately following a dream (KVs 9.23).
And from the object;
ignorance arises from a defect of the sense faculty and from mental conditioning. That is corrupted cognition.
Knowledge is non-defective (KVs 9.27).
The words of the seers and the visions of the perfected ones arise from the dharmas (KVs 9.28).
The inherence of pleasure and pain in the self is the reason for their being distinct entities from the five [objects] and from the qualities that reside therein (KVs 10.1).
Because of the distinction between their respective causes—the desirable and the undesirable—and because of their mutual opposition, pleasure and pain are different entities (KVs 10.2).
Furthermore, the fact that doubt and certainty are different entities is a reason for their being distinct types of cognition (KVs 10.3).
The manner in which these two are produced—through perception and through inference—is also a reason for their being distinct types of cognition (KVs 10.4).
"Has come to be" (*bhūtam*) is explained as that which is perceived directly (*pratyakṣam*).

"Will be" (*bhaviṣyati*) is [so called] because it is seen in another effect (*kāryāntare*). Likewise, "is becoming" (*bhavati*) [is so called] in relation to both those things that are dependent and those that are independent.
"Because it has come into being" means from that which has become [existent] (KVs 10.8).
"And because there is no inherence in the effect while [the cause] exists" (KVs 10.9).
"In one place" means in one [substratum], because [the quality] is observed among other causes that are inherent in the same object (KVs 10.10).
The head, the back, the belly, and the hand [are causes] because they are specific instances thereof (KVs_10.11).
"Cause" [is predicated] of a substance because the effect inheres in it (KVs_10.12),
or because of its conjunction [with the effect] (KVs_10.13).
[The inherence of action] is in the effect due to inherence in the cause;
likewise, [the inherence of color] is in the effect due to inherence in the cause of the cause;
and [the inherence of conjunction] is in the effect due to inherence in the cause.
Likewise, [inference arises] from inherence in the cause and from inherence in the non-cause. (KVs 10.17) From inherence in that which is conjoined, there is the specific quality of fire.
(KVs 10.18) Thus, the means of valid cognition known as inference has been explained. (KVs 10.19)
The performance of those [actions] whose purpose is seen, in the absence of that seen purpose, leads to prosperity.
Because of that statement, the authority of the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is established. (KVs 10.20–21)
